newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada charges Saudi was a driver in Saudi bombing.
newsitem.headline: Canada charges Saudi was a driver in Saudi bombing.

text.p: The Canadian government charged on Thursday that one of two Saudi dissidents it is holding was a driver involved in the massive truck bomb in Saudi Arabia last June that killed 19 U.S. airmen.

In documents filed with the Federal Court, Canada's intelligence service alleged that Hani Abdel-Rahim Hussein al-Sayegh conducted surveillance at the site of the bombing, which also wounded close to 400 people.
It said he then drove a car which "signalled the explosives-laden truck to enter the parking lot."
Sayegh was arrested in Ottawa on March 18 on the grounds that he represented a security threat to Canada.

Federal Court Justice Donna McGillis made an initial examination of the evidence in his absence on Thursday and declined to set him free, fixing a further hearing for April 28 to which he is invited to appear.
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) said last Saturday it wanted to put questions about the bombing to Sayegh, a 28-year-old Shi'ite Muslim who denies being in Saudi Arabia last June.

If, after Sayegh has an opportunity to present the case, McGillis agrees with the federal government's submission that he is a security risk to Canada, then he would most likely be ordered out of Canada at a subsequent immigration hearing.

The document filed by the government with the court said the Canadian Security Intelligence Service had reasonable grounds to believe that Sayegh was a member of Saudi Hizbollah or Hizbollah al-Hijazi.
It described this entity as being born of the fundamentalist group Hizbollah -- which means Party of Allah or Party of God -- that is based in Lebanon.

The statement said that of the known conspirators in the bombing, Jaafar Chueikhat was dead supposedly after committing suicide in a Syrian prison, Ahmed Ibrahim Ahmad al-Mughassil has been identified as the mastermind, and Sayegh conducted the surveillance and drove the car directing the truck.
"Al Sayegh is a member of Saudi Hizbollah who has participated in a lethal terrorist act in Saudi Arabia," the document filed with the court said.

A second Saudi, Fahad al-Shehri, is being held in the same Ottawa prison on charges of terrorism, which he also denies. But the government is focusing on his activities in Afghanistan, Azerbaijan and Bosnia rather than Saudi Arabia.
The Saudi blast took place during the night on June 25 at the Khobar Towers, a complex housing U.S. military personnel outside Dhahran in the oil-rich eastern part of the country.
"On the night of June 25, 1996, a white car followed by a 5,000-gallon (190,000 litre) tanker truck pulled into a parking lot in front of the Al Khobar Towers," the Canadian statement said.

"The white car flashed its headlights and another car already parked in the lot flashed its headlights in response. The two vehicles then pulled into the parking lot. The white car pulled ahead and then stopped.
"The tanker truck, rigged with an estimated 5,000 pounds (2,260 kg) of explosives, was backed up to the fence line in front of the building," the statement continued.

"Two men jumped out of the truck and hurriedly went over and entered the white car, which drove away at high speed. They were quickly followed by the signal vehicle. Four to six minutes later, the truck bomb exploded without warning."

It continued: "Hani Al Sayegh, who is now in Canada, conducted surveillance at the site of the bombing. On the day of the bombing, he was the driver of the car which signalled the explosives-laden truck to enter the parking lot."
The statement added that at the site of the bombing, the Saudis found a detonator similar to a kind used in the past by the Lebanese Hizbollah.
Sayegh told reporters he was in Syria at the time. He arrived in Canada applying to be a refugee from Saudi Arabia because of the way the Sunni Muslim rulers treat Shi'ites.
The Iranian Embassy in Ottawa issued a statement on Wednesday night denying any links with Sayegh, who undertook religious studies in mainly Shi'ite Iran, or the bombing.
